newsitem.title: TURKEY: Iran's Rafsanjani in Turkey on four-day visit.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Rafsanjani in Turkey on four-day visit.

text.p: Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani began a four-day visit to Turkey on Thursday designed to build on growing trade links despite U.S. efforts to isolate Tehran.
The visit marks a further step forward in strengthening ties between the two neighbouring Moslem countries since Necmettin Erbakan became Turkey's first Islamist prime minister in June.

"I believe the subjects we will talk about here will benefit our countries and people," Rafsanjani said after being met by Turkish President Suleyman Demirel and a salute of cannons at Ankara airport.

After joining the Iranian leader for a full military inspection, Demirel told reporters: "I believe that we will achieve important results during Mr Rafsanjani's visit in terms of developing economic and trade relations."
The visit is likely to antagonise the United States which is a close ally of NATO member Turkey and is trying to isolate Iran, which it accuses of sponsoring terrorism.

A senior Turkish official told Reuters details of a preliminary study on construction of a pipeline to carry Iranian oil to Western markets through Turkey's Mediterranean terminal of Ceyhan would be discussed during the visit.
Turkey signed a $23 billion agreement for the supply of Iranian natural gas over 23 years during a visit by Erbakan to Iran in August on his first major trip abroad as prime minister.
The deal was struck days after U.S. President Bill Clinton signed a law imposing sanctions on any company investing over $40 million a year in the energy industries of Iran or Libya.
Ankara said the pipeline deal would not be affected by U.S. sanctions because Turkey was only constructing the stretch of pipeline on its own territory.

The first stage of the deal was initiated last week with the announcement of a tender to construct a 300-km (190-mile) stretch of pipeline from Turkey's Dogubeyazit on the Iranian border to the town of Erzurum. A further 800-km (500-mile) pipline from Erzurum to Ankara is to be built later.
Iranian and Turkish economy officials have been meeting in Ankara this week on new agreements on trade, shipping and the foundation of a joint chamber of commerce.
Turkey is aiming to reach a bilateral trade volume of around $2 billion with Iran within two years from $957 million in 1995, and narrow last year's $421 million trade deficit.

Rafsanjani, who arrived with a large delegation including the foreign and oil ministers, was quoted by the Iranian news agency IRNA as saying his talks would cover the latest developments in the Gulf and Kurdish-controlled northern Iraq.
Relations between the two countries have been strained by concerns in Ankara that Kurdish separatists, seeking self-rule in southeast Turkey, have used Iran as a springboard for attacks.
Demirel said talks would include matters of order, security and "the struggle against terrorism".
Iran, like much of the Moslem world, was angered earlier this year when Turkey signed a deal with Israel, allowing Israeli air force planes to train in Turkish airspace.
Erbakan has dropped a pledge made before he came to power to cancel the accord. This month Turkey signed a $600 million agreement with Israel on the modernisation of Turkish F-4 fighter-bombers.
